caption: A CMC scientist asks WHY a regulatory limit is the number it is — and what work produced it.

answer.question: Why is the mutagenic-impurity acceptable intake set at 1.5 µg/day, and what work produced that number?
answer.summary: rationale question · grade=moderate · 3/4 claims grounded · 1 boundary note(s)

claims.text: What the standard states (the requirement itself): A Threshold of Toxicological Concern (TTC)-based acceptable intake of 1.5 micrograms per person per day for a mutagenic impurity is used as a default to derive a control limit for most pharmaceuticals, taken to be associated with negligible risk. This is the normative acceptance position; it states the limit, not its full derivation.

sources.title: ICH M7 — mutagenic-impurity acceptable intake (TTC)
sources.citation: ICH M7(R2), Assessment and Control of DNA-Reactive (Mutagenic) Impurities

sources.title: ICH Q3A/Q3B — impurity reporting / identification / qualification thresholds
sources.citation: ICH Q3A(R2) Impurities in New Drug Substances (dose-dependent thresholds)

claims.text: Why a limit of this kind exists (documented mechanism): The exact derivation of the cancer TTC is not settled science: peer-reviewed work critiques the statistical derivation of the 1.5 ug/day cancer TTC and recommends structural-class-based limits instead. So 'why exactly 1.5 ug/day' has a grounded derivation AND an active scientific debate — both must be surfaced, not one asserted as final.

sources.title: Peer-reviewed critique of the cancer-TTC derivation
sources.citation: Critique of the derivation of the cancer TTC and recommendations for structural-class-based limits (Regul. Toxicol. Pharmacol.)

claims.text: How the specific figure was arrived at (process, not a re-derivation): Unlike many pragmatic limits, the TTC figure HAS a documented quantitative derivation: 1.5 ug/day corresponds to a theoretical 10^-5 (1 in 100,000) excess lifetime cancer risk. It is obtained by simple linear extrapolation from the TD50 (dose giving 50% tumour incidence) for the most sensitive species and tumour site, across a carcinogenicity analysis of >1000 chemicals; the TTC concept itself originated as the US FDA 'threshold of regulation' for food-contact substances. The methods are regarded as conservative.

Need to confirm — my own guess.” Treat as a hypothesis to confirm, not a confirmed result.

answer.question: What hERG limit must a compound pass before it can progress?
answer.summary: normative question · grade=high · 1/2 claims grounded · 0 boundary note(s)

claims.text: The applicable requirement: There is NO single regulatory hERG 'threshold' a compound must pass. Proarrhythmic cardiac risk is assessed under ICH S7B (nonclinical in-vitro IKr/hERG + in-vivo QT) and ICH E14 (clinical QT/QTc), as an integrated risk assessment, not a pass/fail number. The commonly quoted ~10 uM hERG screening value is an empirical DISCOVERY heuristic (a safety-margin rule of thumb versus free Cmax), not a regulatory acceptance limit.
